explanations.explanation: Bethlehem is it. The LORD says, “I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem…” Samuel, the LORD's prophet, gets a town AND a name. That's more direction than I get from my own memory when I walk into a room and forget why.

Hebron is a fine-sounding town, friend, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, “I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem…” Samuel gets a clear address, and a clear address is a gift. Keep Bethlehem in your pocket for this one.

Gibeah doesn't show up in what the LORD says here. He tells Samuel, “I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem…” So the stop is Bethlehem, and Jesse is the man to see. I'd have mixed up the town names too, honestly, so no shame in that.

explanations.answer: He has picked a king from Jesse's sons
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The LORD says, “…for I have selected from his sons a king for Myself.” So the trip isn't random. The LORD already knows what He's doing, and Samuel just has to go and see it.

explanations.answer: He wants Jesse's sons to join the army
explanations.explanation: An army never comes up in the LORD's words. He says He has selected a king from Jesse's sons. Samuel isn't going to recruit anybody. He's going because the LORD has picked a king for Himself.

explanations.answer: He wants Samuel to settle in Jesse's town
explanations.explanation: Moving in isn't the plan. The LORD sends Samuel because He has selected a king from Jesse's sons. And at the end of the passage, Samuel sets out and goes to Ramah. He's a visitor, friend, not a new neighbor.

Samuel says it straight: “Saul will hear of it and kill me!” Saul is the king the LORD has rejected, and Samuel is afraid of what he'd do. That's a heavy thing to say out loud. You can hear how serious Samuel is, so the LORD gives him a plan right after.
Jail doesn't come up. Samuel says, “Saul will hear of it and kill me!” That's a much bigger fear than a locked door. I think Samuel is truly scared here, and the LORD answers him with a plan.
Samuel never mentions banishment. His words are, “Saul will hear of it and kill me!” That's a heavy moment, friend. The LORD answers Samuel and gives him something to do about it.

True. The LORD says, “…and I will show you what you are to do. You are to anoint for Me the one I indicate.” Samuel doesn't have to guess which son. The LORD is going to point him out, and that's a relief for anybody who has ever picked the wrong box at a bakery sale.

The text says the opposite. The LORD says, “…and I will show you what you are to do. You are to anoint for Me the one I indicate.” So Samuel isn't left to figure out the son on his own. The LORD is the one who will indicate him.

Right, they ask, “Do you come in peace?” They tremble when they ask it. Samuel answers, “In peace,” and then tells them he has come to sacrifice to the LORD. A little trembling in front of a prophet is something I understand, friend, because my mustache does it when the oven timer goes off.
The elders don't ask about Saul. They tremble and ask, “Do you come in peace?” Their question is about Samuel himself. Samuel answers, “In peace.”

explanations.answer: Who else is coming with you
explanations.explanation: They don't ask about anyone else. The elders meet Samuel trembling and ask, “Do you come in peace?” Samuel answers with “In peace,” and then says he has come to sacrifice to the LORD.
Not quite, friend. The text says Samuel “…consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.” So the sons are consecrated and invited right along with their father.

False is right. The text says Samuel “…consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.” The sons are invited right along with their father. That's the moment everything is set up for the choosing.

explanations.answer: Surely this one is the LORD's anointed
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. Samuel sees Eliab and says, “Surely here before the LORD is His anointed.” Samuel sounds sure, friend, REAL sure. And the LORD is about to have a word with him.

explanations.answer: Surely this one is too young to lead
explanations.explanation: Samuel says nothing about Eliab being too young. His words are, “Surely here before the LORD is His anointed.” I think he's seeing a king, not a problem. And the LORD answers him next.

explanations.answer: Surely this one must offer the sacrifice
explanations.explanation: The sacrifice isn't what Samuel is talking about. He says, “Surely here before the LORD is His anointed.” He thinks he's found the one to anoint. The LORD has other plans.

The heart. The LORD says, “For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.” I've stamped a cookie that looked gorgeous and tasted like nothing, and I've stamped a lopsided one that was the best in the batch. The LORD looks at what's inside every time.

Strength isn't what the LORD names. He says, “For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.” People notice what's on the outside, and the LORD looks deeper. It's a good thing to keep in mind next time you're sizing somebody up.

The family line isn't in His words. The LORD says, “For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.” He sets outward appearance next to the heart. Earlier He tells Samuel, “Do not consider his appearance or height…”
Not this time, friend. When Jesse presents Abinadab, Samuel says, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.” The word either tells you Abinadab isn't the first one passed over. The line keeps moving.
False is right. Samuel says, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.” Abinadab walks up, and Abinadab walks away. Jesse still has more sons to bring.

Seven it is. The text says, “Thus Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel…” Samuel tells him, “The LORD has not chosen any of these.” That's a whole row of sons and not one of them is the one. I'd have needed a bigger room.

Five is short. The text says Jesse “…made seven of his sons pass before Samuel…” That's two more than you counted, and still not the chosen one. Samuel tells him, “The LORD has not chosen any of these.”

Ten is too many. The text says Jesse “…made seven of his sons pass before Samuel…” After that, Jesse says there is still the youngest, who is tending the sheep. So seven is the count of sons who pass before Samuel.

Sons. Samuel asks, “Are these all the sons you have?” The LORD has chosen one of Jesse's sons, and seven have passed without being chosen. So Samuel checks if there are any left. Smart question, friend.

Servants aren't who he's asking about. Samuel asks, “Are these all the sons you have?” The LORD said the king comes from Jesse's sons. So Samuel checks on the sons, and that question changes everything.
Nephews don't come up. Samuel asks, “Are these all the sons you have?” The LORD has selected a king from Jesse's sons, so that's the list Samuel wants to finish. And it turns out there's one more.
True. Samuel says, “Send for him… For we will not sit down to eat until he arrives.” The meal waits for the youngest. I'd say that's some serious confidence from Samuel.
The text says the opposite. Samuel says, “Send for him… For we will not sit down to eat until he arrives.” So the eating waits for the youngest.

That's what the LORD says: “Rise and anoint him, for he is the one.” After seven sons and a wait, the answer is plain. The LORD tells Samuel which one, just like He said He would. I think the whole room was holding its breath, like when the oven door opens.
No more waiting. The LORD says, “Rise and anoint him, for he is the one.” The youngest is the last one Jesse sends for, and he's the one. Samuel can get up and get moving.

explanations.answer: Send him back to the field
explanations.explanation: Back to the field isn't what the LORD says. His words are, “Rise and anoint him, for he is the one.” The youngest was out with the sheep, and now he's right where the LORD wants him. Samuel is told to anoint him.

The Spirit of the LORD. The text says, “…the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward.” David is the youngest son, the one who was tending the sheep. Samuel anointed him in the presence of his brothers, and from that day forward the Spirit rushed upon him.
That fear belonged to Samuel earlier. He said, “Saul will hear of it and kill me!” (1 Samuel 16:2) But what rushes upon David is “…the Spirit of the LORD…” And it stays “…from that day forward.”

Sorrow for Saul was Samuel's. The LORD asked him, “How long are you going to mourn for Saul…” at the start of this passage. What rushes upon David is “…the Spirit of the LORD…” That happens “…from that day forward.”
